title: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC)
summary: DMARC is a scalable mechanism by which a mail-originating organization can express domain-level policies and preferences for message validation, disposition, and reporting, which a receiving organization can use to improve handling of mail. This informational document was replaced by RFC 9989, RFC 9990, and RFC 9991.

plainLanguage.summary: DMARC lets the owner of an email domain set rules for what a receiving mail service should do with a message that claims to come from that domain. The owner publishes the rules in DNS. The receiver then checks whether the message really was sent by that domain, using the SPF or DKIM results, and applies the rules when it was not. The receiver also sends the owner reports saying what it saw.

questions: what is the dmarc pct tag
subtitle: How a domain owner says what to do with mail that claims to come from it but fails its authentication checks.

tldr.problem: SPF and DKIM let a receiver tell whether a message was authorised by a domain, but there was no common way for a domain owner to say what a receiver should do about mail that fails those checks, nor any way to hear back about what is failing.
tldr.mechanism: A domain owner publishes a policy record in DNS. A receiver compares the domain in the From header with the domain SPF or DKIM authenticated, and if they match the message passes; if not, the receiver applies the published policy and reports the outcome back.
tldr.outcome: The mechanism gives domain owners a way to enforce a policy on their own mail and a way to measure how well it is working. RFC 7489 was obsoleted by RFC 9989, RFC 9990 and RFC 9991.

facts.label: Default alignment mode
facts.value: Relaxed, for both adkim and aspf

today: RFC 7489 is Informational and was obsoleted by RFC 9989, RFC 9990 and RFC 9991. It was updated by RFC 8553 and RFC 8616.

sections.title: What DMARC Does
sections.content:
The Sender Policy Framework and DomainKeys Identified Mail provide domain-level authentication. They enable cooperating email receivers to detect mail authorised to use the domain name, which can permit differential handling. However, there had been no single widely accepted or publicly available mechanism for communicating domain-specific message-handling policies to receivers, or for requesting reporting of the authentication and disposition of received mail. Absent the ability to obtain feedback reports, originators who implemented email authentication had difficulty determining how effective their authentication was, and as a consequence use of authentication failures to filter mail typically did not succeed.

Over time, one-on-one relationships were established between select senders and receivers with privately communicated means to assert policy and receive message traffic and authentication disposition reporting. Although these ad hoc practices were generally successful, they required significant manual coordination between parties, and this model does not scale for general use on the Internet.

DMARC is a mechanism by which email operators leverage existing authentication and policy advertisement technologies to enable both message-stream feedback and enforcement of policies against unauthenticated email. The basic outline has four steps. Domain Owners publish policy assertions about domains via the DNS. Receivers compare the RFC5322.From address in the mail to the SPF and DKIM results, if present, and the DMARC policy in DNS. These receivers can use these results to determine how the mail should be handled. The receiver then sends reports to the Domain Owner or its designee about mail claiming to be from their domain.

DMARC differs from previous approaches to policy advertisement in several ways. Authentication technologies are decoupled from any technology-specific policy mechanism and used solely to establish reliable per-message domain-level identifiers. Multiple authentication technologies are used to reduce the impact of transient authentication errors and of site-specific configuration errors and deployment gaps, and to enable more use cases than any individual technology supports alone. Receiver-generated feedback is supported. And the domain name extracted from the message's RFC5322.From field is the primary identifier in the mechanism.

The RFC is explicit that DMARC does not produce or encourage elevated delivery privilege of authenticated email, and that it is a mechanism for policy distribution enabling increasingly strict handling of messages that fail authentication checks, ranging from no action through altered delivery up to message rejection.
sections.plainLanguage: SPF and DKIM can already tell a receiver whether a message was allowed by a particular domain. What they cannot do is tell the receiver what to do when the answer is no, and they give the domain owner no way to find out what is going wrong. DMARC adds both: a published policy and a feedback channel.

sections.title: Identifier Alignment and the Organizational Domain
sections.content:
Email authentication technologies authenticate various and disparate aspects of an individual message. DKIM authenticates the domain that affixed a signature to the message, while SPF can authenticate either the domain in the SMTP MAIL FROM portion or the HELO domain, or both. These may be different domains, and they are typically not visible to the end user.

DMARC authenticates use of the RFC5322.From domain by requiring that it match, or be aligned with, an authenticated identifier. The From domain was chosen as the central identity because it is a required message header field and therefore guaranteed to be present in compliant messages, and because most mail user agents render it as the originator and show some or all of it to end users. It is therefore the field users use to identify the source of a message, and so a prime target for abuse.

Each underlying authentication technology yields authenticated domains when it succeeds, and each can be operated in a strict mode or a relaxed mode. In relaxed mode, the Organizational Domains of the DKIM-authenticated signing domain, taken from the value of the d= tag, and of the RFC5322.From domain must be equal for the identifiers to be aligned. In strict mode, only an exact match between both fully qualified domain names counts. For example, if a validated DKIM signature verifies with a d= domain of example.com and the From address is alerts@news.example.com, the two are in alignment in relaxed mode but not in strict mode. The same split applies to SPF: in relaxed mode the SPF-authenticated domain and the From domain must have the same Organizational Domain, while in strict mode only an exact DNS domain match counts.

Alignment is required because a message can bear a valid signature from any domain, including a mailing list or a bad actor, so merely bearing a valid signature is not enough to infer authenticity of the Author Domain. A single email can contain multiple DKIM signatures, and it is a DMARC pass if any DKIM signature is aligned and verifies.

The Organizational Domain is found with a four-step algorithm. Acquire a public suffix list, that is, a list of DNS domain names reserved for registrations, which is the union of the country registration rules and the IANA registry of top-level domains. Break the subject domain name into an ordered set of labels, numbered from right to left. Search the public suffix list for the name matching the largest number of labels found in the subject domain, and call that number x. Then construct a new domain name from the matching suffix prefixed with the x+1th label of the subject domain. Since com is an IANA-registered top-level domain, a subject domain of a.b.c.d.example.com has an Organizational Domain of example.com. The process of determining a suffix is currently a heuristic, and no list is guaranteed to be accurate or current.
sections.plainLanguage: The key question is whether the domain that authenticated the message is the same as the domain in the visible From address. In relaxed mode only the registered part has to match, so example.com can vouch for news.example.com. In strict mode the two have to be identical. The registered part is found by taking the domain apart until only the part a person could have registered is left.

sections.title: How a Message Is Checked
sections.content:
Two mechanisms are supported for determining authenticated identifiers. DKIM provides a domain-level identifier in the content of the d= tag of a validated DKIM-Signature header field. SPF can authenticate both the domain found in an SMTP HELO or EHLO command and the domain found in an SMTP MAIL command, and DMARC uses the result of SPF authentication of the MAIL FROM identity.

DMARC policies are published by the Domain Owner and retrieved by the Mail Receiver during the SMTP session, via the DNS. The filtering function is based on whether the RFC5322.From field domain is aligned with an authenticated domain name from SPF or DKIM. When a DMARC policy is published for the domain name found in the From field, and that domain name is not validated through SPF or DKIM, the disposition of that message can be affected by that policy when delivered to a participating receiver. The authentication mechanisms employed by DMARC authenticate only a DNS domain; they do not authenticate the local part of an email address, nor do they validate the legitimacy of message content.

The flow described by the RFC runs as follows. The Domain Owner constructs an SPF policy and publishes it in DNS, configures the system for DKIM signing, and publishes a DMARC message-handling policy via DNS. The author generates a message and hands it to the domain owner's designated mail submission service. The submission service passes the relevant details to the DKIM signing module to generate a signature, and relays the now-signed message to its designated transport service. The message may pass through other relays and eventually arrives at the recipient's transport service. The recipient's delivery service conducts SPF and DKIM authentication checks, each of which requires queries to the Author Domain's DNS data. The results are passed to the DMARC module along with the author's domain, and the module attempts to retrieve a policy from DNS for that domain; if none is found, it determines the Organizational Domain and repeats the attempt. If a policy is found, it is combined with the author's domain and the SPF and DKIM results to produce a DMARC policy result, a pass or a fail, which can optionally cause reports to be generated. The recipient's transport service then either delivers the message or takes other local policy action based on the result, and, when requested, collects data from the delivery session for feedback.
sections.plainLanguage: The check happens at the receiving mail service. It runs SPF and DKIM, looks up the policy in DNS, and compares the domain each check authenticated with the domain in the From address. One aligned pass means the message passes. Otherwise the published policy decides what happens to it, and the details are collected for the reports.

sections.title: The Policy Record and Its Tags
sections.content:
Domain Owner DMARC preferences are stored as DNS TXT records in subdomains named _dmarc. The owner of example.com would post its preferences in a TXT record at _dmarc.example.com, and a receiver querying for mail with a From domain of example.com would issue a TXT query for that subdomain. The data found there is called the DMARC record. Where a TXT record comprises several character-string objects, the module performing DMARC evaluation MUST concatenate them in order and parse the result as a single string.

DMARC records follow the extensible tag-value syntax for DNS-based key records defined in DKIM. Only tags defined in the document or in later extensions are processed, and unknown tags MUST be ignored. The initial set of tags is as follows. The v tag identifies the record as a DMARC record, MUST have the value DMARC1, and MUST be the first tag in the list; if it does not, or is absent, the entire record MUST be ignored. The p tag is the requested Mail Receiver policy and is REQUIRED for policy records. Its value is none, meaning no specific action is requested; quarantine, meaning mail that fails the check should be treated as suspicious, which can mean placing it in a spam folder, scrutinising it with additional intensity, or flagging it; or reject, meaning mail that fails should be rejected, which SHOULD occur during the SMTP transaction. The sp tag sets the policy for subdomains and is ignored when the record is published on a subdomain of an Organizational Domain.

The adkim and aspf tags say whether strict or relaxed alignment is required for DKIM and for SPF, each defaulting to r for relaxed, with s meaning strict. The pct tag is a percentage between 0 and 100, defaulting to 100, saying how much of the owner's mail stream the policy applies to; it MUST NOT be applied to the DMARC-generated reports, which must be sent and received unhindered, and its purpose is to allow a slow rollout of enforcement. The ri tag is the interval requested between aggregate reports, a 32-bit unsigned integer defaulting to 86400 seconds; implementations MUST be able to provide daily reports and SHOULD be able to provide hourly ones when asked. The rua and ruf tags list the addresses to which aggregate feedback and message-specific failure information are to be sent; a receiver MUST implement support for a mailto: URI, and if the tag is not provided, MUST NOT generate the corresponding reports. The fo tag gives failure reporting options, and its content MUST be ignored if a ruf tag is not also specified. The rf tag names the report format for per-message failure reports, and for interoperability the Authentication Failure Reporting Format MUST be supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The policy lives in one DNS text record under the name _dmarc at the domain. It is a list of tags: which policy to apply, whether to apply it to all mail or only some, how strict the domain match must be, where to send reports, and how often. The version tag has to be first and has to read DMARC1, or the whole record is ignored.

sections.title: Feedback Reports
sections.content:
The aggregate feedback report is designed to give Domain Owners precise insight into authentication results, corrective action that needs to be taken by Domain Owners, and the effect of the owner's policy on the email streams processed by Mail Receivers. Visibility comes in the form of daily or more frequent receiver-originated feedback reports containing aggregate data on message streams relevant to the Domain Owner, including messages that passed DMARC authentication as well as those that did not.

The report SHOULD include the DMARC policy discovered and applied, if any, the selected message disposition, the identifier evaluated by SPF and its result, the identifier evaluated by DKIM and its result, for both an indication of whether the identifier was in alignment, data for each of the owner's subdomains separately from mail from the Organizational Domain even where there is no explicit subdomain policy, the sending and receiving domains, the policy requested and the policy actually applied if different, the number of successful authentications, and the counts of messages based on all messages received even if their delivery is ultimately blocked by other filtering agents.

Alongside the aggregate reports, a receiver may generate per-message reports containing information about individual messages that fail SPF and/or DKIM. Per-message failure reports are a useful source of information when debugging deployments, if messages can be determined to be legitimate even though they failed authentication, or in analysing attacks. The capability is enabled by DMARC but defined in other referenced material.
sections.plainLanguage: The reports come in two kinds. The aggregate report is a periodic summary of what the receiver saw for a domain: how many messages passed, how many failed, and which way each failed. The failure report is about one message at a time and is useful when working out why a legitimate message failed.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Aggregate reports are limited in scope to DMARC policy and disposition results, to information about the underlying authentication mechanisms, and to the identifiers involved in validation. Failed-message reporting provides message-specific details, and individual reports can contain message content as well as trace header fields. Both report types may expose sender and recipient identifiers, and although the format used for failed-message reporting supports redaction, it is capable of exposing the entire message to the report recipient.

Domain Owners requesting reports receive information about mail claiming to be from them, which includes mail that was not in fact from them, so information about the final destination of mail, where it might otherwise be obscured by intermediate systems, is exposed. Where message-forwarding arrangements exist, the owner also receives information about mail forwarded to domains that were not originally on the recipient list, so destination domains previously unknown to the owner may become visible. Disclosure of information about the messages is requested by the entity generating the email in the first place, the Domain Owner and not the Mail Receiver, and for some providers this is treated similarly to complaint reporting about spamming or phishing. Report generators are encouraged to review their reporting limitations under such policies before enabling DMARC reporting. A DMARC record can also specify that reports be sent to an intermediary operating on behalf of the Domain Owner, and receipt of such data by third parties may or may not be permitted by the Mail Receiver's privacy policy.

On security, the URIs published in DNS TXT records are well-understood possible targets for attack, and Domain Owners will need to harden these addresses against high-volume denial-of-service attacks, against deliberately constructed malformed reports intended to identify or exploit parsing or processing vulnerabilities, and against reports containing false claims for the Submitter or Reported-Domain fields, including data from compromised but known receivers. Because the DMARC mechanism and its underlying technologies depend on the security of the DNS, serious consideration should be given to deploying DNSSEC in parallel with DMARC by both Domain Owners and Mail Receivers. The RFC also warns about display-name attacks, where the address in the From field is genuine but the display name beside it is misleading.
sections.plainLanguage: Reporting leaks a little. The owner of a domain learns which addresses claim to be from it and where that mail went, which can expose mail that was never theirs and destination domains they did not know about. Per-message reports can carry the whole message. The report addresses in DNS are also an attack surface, so they need the same care as any other published address.

messages.label: MESSAGE
messages.note: The author hands the message to the domain owner's submission service.

messages.label: SIGNED MESSAGE
messages.note: The submission service adds a DKIM signature and relays the message.

messages.label: MESSAGE
messages.note: The message arrives at the recipient's transport service.

messages.label: SPF AND DKIM RESULTS
messages.note: The results, together with the From domain, go to the DMARC module.

messages.label: PASS OR FAIL
messages.note: The module looks the policy up in DNS and returns the result, which decides the disposition.

viz.caption: THE DMARC TAGS AND WHAT EACH ONE SETS

items.title: v
items.text: Version. Required, must be first, and must read DMARC1 or the record is ignored.

items.title: p
items.text: The requested policy: none, quarantine or reject. Required in a policy record.

items.title: sp
items.text: The requested policy for subdomains, when it differs from p.

items.title: adkim and aspf
items.text: Whether DKIM and SPF alignment must be strict or relaxed. The default is relaxed.

items.title: pct
items.text: The percentage of the owner's mail the policy applies to. The default is 100.

items.title: ri
items.text: How often to send aggregate reports. The default is 86400 seconds.

items.title: rua and ruf
items.text: Where to send aggregate reports and per-message failure reports.

viz.caption: THE THREE VALUES OF THE p TAG

items.label: NONE
items.desc: The domain owner requests no specific action about delivery.

items.label: QUARANTINE
items.desc: Mail that fails the check should be treated as suspicious: a spam folder, closer scrutiny, or a flag.

items.label: REJECT
items.desc: Mail that fails the check should be rejected, and rejection should happen during the SMTP transaction.
